rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The elution window will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity adjustments.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient one step to test whether full resolution can be retained with faster elution, keeping the original method as the proven optimum.

The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair close to the resolution threshold. Raise temperature one step to test whether faster elution and a selectivity shift preserve full resolution.
Test the next shorter gradient at the temperature that improved the critical pair. This probes the speed limit for full resolution while retaining injection 3 as a maximum-score fallback.

Narrow the gradient window to restore a slope close to the fully resolving 8-minute method, while increasing starting organic to reduce initial retention. This tests whether the critical pair can regain full resolution in a shorter run.

Raise temperature one step: the earlier temperature test improved the critical pair while shortening retention. Only a small resolution gain is needed to reach maximum CRF with this narrower, faster method.

Increase starting organic one step to shorten elution while slightly reducing gradient steepness, which may improve the critical middle pair. Monitor the first pair for loss of resolution as its retention decreases.

Raise starting organic to accelerate elution and lower the endpoint to make the gradient shallower, aiming to protect the marginal middle pair. The first pair remains a key check as the early peaks approach the unretained region.

Lower the endpoint one step to soften the gradient and recover the small resolution deficit in the middle pair. Keep starting organic and temperature fixed to avoid further compressing the early pair.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a substantially steeper gradient for a faster alternative beyond the middle-pair co-elution region. The strong slope response suggests that pair may reverse order and separate again; all six peaks should still elute well within the acquisition window.

Test the temperature dependence of the unresolved pairs under the fast gradient. Lower temperature previously favored early-pair separation and may improve the middle pair after its apparent order reversal, while the run remains comfortably below 10 minutes.

Return to the fully resolving narrow-window approach with a 4-minute gradient whose slope is only slightly steeper than injection 9. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, aiming to preserve maximum CRF with slightly faster elution.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to preserve middle-pair separation. Lower temperature should help retain and separate the early pair, which is approaching the unretained region.

Make the gradient shallower and raise temperature one step to improve the unresolved middle pair from injection 13. The early pair has some resolution margin, and the lower endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Return near the fastest fully resolved conditions and test a slightly steeper slope than injection 7 using a trimmed endpoint. This probes whether the middle pair can retain R ≥ 1.5 while reducing the last-peak time.
Raise temperature one step to try to recover the small middle-pair resolution deficit and shorten elution. Monitor the early pair closely, since previous temperature increases reduced its separation.

Test a short, shallow gradient followed by a hold, aiming to preserve middle-pair separation before the hold accelerates the remaining elution relative to staying at low organic. This explores a different timing strategy while retaining injection 12 as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Lower starting organic and soften the gradient relative to injection 16 to recover early-pair resolution at 55 C. This tests whether elevated temperature can support a fully resolved method with more middle-pair margin.

Back off the endpoint one grid step from injection 15 to recover middle-pair resolution, and return to 50 C to protect the early pair. This targets maximum CRF with greater resolution margin near the fastest proven methods.

Test a shallower gradient at 45 C to strengthen early-pair separation while compensating for the temperature-related loss in middle-pair resolution. This seeks a maximum-score alternative with more balanced resolution margins than injection 12.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 20 to shorten elution while testing its middle-pair resolution margin. This also checks whether the fastest proven gradient remains fully resolving at a lower temperature that better separates the early pair.

Raise temperature one step from the fully resolved injection 20 to shorten retention while preserving its middle-pair margin. The early pair remained above R = 1.5 under nearby conditions at 50 C, making this a promising maximum-score method with balanced resolution margins.

Lower temperature one step from injection 19 to strengthen early-pair separation while testing whether its middle-pair margin remains sufficient. This targets another maximum-score method with useful resolution margins; injection 12 remains the fastest proven fully resolved option.

Raise the endpoint one step from injection 17 to shorten the last peak’s hold-phase retention. This tests whether its middle-pair resolution margin can tolerate the steeper two-minute gradient, with injection 12 retained as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Use the final injection to test a shallower neighbor of injection 19, targeting stronger middle-pair resolution while preserving early-pair separation and elution well below 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured; injection 12 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.
